If you step back, this bleak July jobs report means the labor market is stalling again.

Average job gains past 3 months: 20k
Average job gains past 6 months: 44k
Average job gains past 12 months: 26k
Average job gains in all of 2025: 10k

The strong jobs reports earlier this year have now faded. A "no hire" job market is one with few opportunities and little dynamism.

posts.text:
This worries me...  Over 2.1 million people have left the U.S. labor force since November.

Labor force participation rate November: 62.5%
Labor force participation rate now (July): 61.4%

Some of this is due to lower immigration. Some due to Baby Boomers retiring, but it also likely signals job seekers becoming discouraged.

Prime-age labor force participation for workers ages 25 to 54 looks a little better, but even that has fallen sharply
posts.summary: Large labor force exodus signals job-seeking concerns beyond retirement trends

The financial squeeze is real for many Americans right now.

Wage growth is *not* contributing to inflation right now. That means many workers will struggle in the months ahead.

American consumers are increasingly concerned about AI.
It’s even showing up in the University of Michigan consumer sentiment survey

10% of respondents spontaneously mentioned AI.

"On balance, negative comments on AI outweigh positive comments," Hsu said.
"Still, at this time, AI is far less important for consumer views of the economy than gasoline prices, mentioned by nearly one-third of consumers.”

New Chair Kevin Warsh sounds slightly hawkish again today, but it's notable how often he keeps referring to the "full range of alternatives" on monetary policy.

He keeps emphasizing more than just rate hikes

"If I look at the Treasury curve, If I look at the dollar…what they’re broadly saying is this committee does own it and has the credibility to deliver it and they believe, like I do, that we will."
posts.summary: Fed Chair emphasizing multiple monetary policy tools beyond rate hikes

posts.text:
Good to hear new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh say the 2% inflation target remains firmly in place.

"There is no soft inflation target. There is no soft implicit target, not on this committee’s watch. There’s only a target, and it’s 2%," Warsh says.
posts.summary: Approves Fed's commitment to strict 2% inflation target

JUST IN: Federal Reserve keeps the benchmark interest rate the same (3.5 to 3.75%). That's where it's been since December.

But look at the vote: 9 in favor, 3 against.

All 3 dissenters wanted to HIKE interest rates today.
